newsitem.title: GERMANY: Karstadt group sales down Jan-March. [corrected 12:43 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Karstadt group sales down Jan-March. [corrected 12:43 GMT]

text.p: German stores group Karstadt AG's group sales fell 2.3 percent in the first three months (corrects from five months) of this year to 5.979 billion marks ($3.5 billion), chief executive Walter Deuss told a news conference on Thursday.

Deuss declined to give any details of group profits during the January-March (corrects period from January-May) period but said Karstadt was seeking to achieve a "significant improvement" in its results this year.
He also said Karstadt wanted to treble its pre-tax return on sales this year from last year's 0.24 percent, with the long-term goal of reaching 3.4-percent returns, last achieved in 1990.

The Karstadt group's results have been weighed by the loss-making Hertie department store chain acquired three years ago, but Deuss said he expected the Hertie unit to come close to breaking even this year.
Hertie posted a net loss last year of 102.2 million marks, down from a loss of 118.9 million marks the year before, Karstadt's annual report said.
But accounting for losses carried forward, the bottom-line 1996 loss at Hertie was 241.4 million marks.

The Karstadt group posted a net profit in 1996 of 114 million marks, down from 189.2 million, but earnings per share based on the DVFA accounting standard, or the German financial analyst evaluation method, came out at minus 20.92 marks.

Deuss said the negative earnings per share figure had arisen because the costs of carrying out store closures counted in the DVFA accounting method, while windfall profits from related asset disposals were excluded.

Deuss said that had these factors been taken into account, the company would have reported earnings per share of 39 pfennigs rather than a 20.92 marks loss (clarifies Deuss' prediction of earnings per share).

Karstadt management has proposed a cut in the 1996 dividend to 10 marks from 13 marks per share due to its weaker earnings position, but Deuss said he hoped to be able to make a higher payout in the future.
"We have reached a basis upon which we can build," Deuss told reporters.
